summary: Through the Clouds is an interactive geospatial analysis web application and data pipeline designed to monitor environmental disasters across Indonesia using NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) data.   During critical events like forest fires and volcanic eruptions, thick smoke and cloud cover severely blind traditional optical imaging satellites. Our solution addresses this challenge by processing NISAR L2 radar datasets (GCOV, GUNW, and SME2), which penetrate atmospheric obstructions to capture ground-level changes. We validated this approach across three major Indonesian case studies: isolating volcanic surface deformation on Anak Krakatau (-8.7Σ coherence drop), tracking severe peatland soil moisture loss (-33%) in Central Kalimantan prior to fire season, and mapping post-fire canopy loss in West Kalimantan that correlated 9.2× higher with NASA VIIRS thermal hotspots. Additionally, we transparently benchmarked three negative test cases to define radar detection boundaries against signal noise and small-scale changes.
details:
Through the Clouds combines an automated geospatial processing pipeline with an interactive web visualization platform to analyze surface changes across Indonesia using NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) data. Unlike traditional optical satellites that are blinded by thick smoke and tropical cloud cover, NISAR's L-band radar penetrates atmospheric obstructions to measure physical ground conditions. The platform processes three core NISAR Level-2 products—GUNW (radar coherence for surface stability), SME2 (soil moisture estimates), and GCOV (radar backscatter for forest canopy structure)—and cross-references them against external thermal hotspot data from NASA FIRMS VIIRS and optical imagery from MODIS Aqua.

Key Benefits & Intended Impact

  • All-Weather Disaster Intelligence: Provides continuous, cloud-penetrating monitoring of volcanic eruptions, peatland drought conditions, and forest fire scars in tropical regions where optical imagery frequently fails.
  • Cross-Sensor Validation: Demonstrates strong statistical alignment between independent sensors—such as isolating a sharp radar coherence collapse on Anak Krakatau while three neighboring islands remained stable, and confirming over nine times greater radar canopy loss directly beneath VIIRS fire detections in West Kalimantan.
  • Actionable Early Warning & Mitigation: Empowers disaster response agencies, environmental researchers, and policymakers to identify high-risk dry peatlands (such as Central Kalimantan losing a third of its soil moisture) and assess burn severity faster, supporting more targeted resource allocation and environmental protection.

Tools, Datasets & Technologies Used

  • Satellite & Geospatial Datasets: NISAR L2 (GCOV, GUNW, SME2 via NASA/ISRO ASF DAAC), NASA FIRMS VIIRS active fire detections, MODIS Aqua imagery (via NASA Worldview), and Sentinel-2 cloudless 2024 base maps (by EOX IT Services).
  • Software & Development Stack: Custom data processing scripts (Python-based geospatial workflows) to extract statistical metrics and generate map layers, paired with a lightweight front-end web application hosted via GitHub Pages (yumikopubangelo.github.io/through-the-clouds) and version-controlled on GitHub.
  • AI Development Assistance: Claude (Anthropic) was utilized to assist in writing and debugging the data analysis scripts, with all final statistical outputs derived directly from processed NISAR datasets.

Creativity & Team Considerations Rather than presenting radar as an infallible silver bullet, our team took a scientific honesty and boundary-testing approach. Alongside three successful case studies (Anak Krakatau, Central Kalimantan drought, and West Kalimantan fire scars), we explicitly tested and published three negative results out of six total experiments: Jakarta land subsidence (masked by signal noise over 84 days), fire early warning direction errors, the Flores M7.7 earthquake (where localized damage covered only about 56 out of 7.6 million pixels), and a false alarm at Cirata Dam (where an anomaly in one viewing angle was not confirmed in the second). By contrasting neighboring control islands, comparing multiple radar viewing angles, and transparently reporting where radar fails on small, slow, or scattered events, our project builds genuine operational trust in when and how NISAR data should be relied upon.
